newsitem.title: USA: Saudi suspect said ready to ask for U.S. asylum.
newsitem.headline: Saudi suspect said ready to ask for U.S. asylum.

text.p: On the eve of a court hearing for a Saudi suspect in the bombing that killed 19 U.S. airmen in Saudi Arabia last year, his lawyer said on Tuesday he is ready to file a request for political asylum in the United States.
Michael Wildes, immigration lawyer for Hani al-Sayegh, said he had drawn up papers requesting political asylum and was ready to file them at his client's request.
Sayegh, 29, is accused of acting as the driver and lookout in the June 1996 attack on Khobar Towers, a U.S. military housing complex in Saudi Arabia.

He was arrested in Canada and deported to the United States on June 17 after striking a deal with U.S. officials under which he would plead guilty to lesser charges arising from an unrelated anti-American plot hatched in the Middle East but never carried out.
But questions have arisen about whether Sayegh will abandon the still-secret agreement, under which he would cooperate with U.S. authorities and tell them what he knows about the bombing.

After two previous delays, Sayegh is due to appear before U.S. District Judge Emmet Sullivan for a status hearing at 10 a.m. EDT (1400 GMT) on Wednesday. Wildes earlier this month said Sayegh was reconsidering the agreement.
He declined on Tuesday to say how his client would plead.
Sayegh's court-appointed criminal attorney did not return telephone calls, and the Justice Department had no comment.

Wildes told Reuters late on Tuesday that his client -- a member of the Shiite Moslem minority in Saudi Arabia -- still feared being returned to his country, and that he denied any involvement in the Khobar Towers bombing.
"He does not know anything or know who perpetrated this atrocity," Wildes said, describing Sayegh as a religious studies student who had visited Iran's holy sites.
Sayegh was considering requesting asylum in the United States because he "really feels he was set up by Saudi intelligence to take a fall for this bombing," Wildes said.
The attorney said Saudi intelligence agents had attempted to contact Sayegh in Canada, but "he stopped it," and Sayegh believed they had also tried to contact him in Washington.

Wildes said the asylum request would force the U.S. government to review Sayegh's case, although he noted that a conviction on the conspiracy charge being reviewed on Wednesday would provide a basis for denying the request.
